changes.before: Define a `fill` keyframe animation from zero width to full width.
changes.after: Animate a bar while keeping its final result easy to read.

before: An animation changes a style over time. CSS keyframes define the starting, ending, and possibly middle values. animation applies those keyframes to an element. A progress display also needs understandable information when the motion is absent. Keep a visible text label with the final result, rather than expecting someone to judge a bar's width. This exercise animates an already-complete result for presentation; CSS by itself does not know whether an actual upload has completed. A real progress display would receive its value from the work being done.

The animation name must match the @keyframes name exactly. A duration gives how long one run takes. A timing function describes how the visual change moves through that run. linear moves evenly; ease-out slows near the end. both is a fill mode: it applies the starting frame during any delay and keeps the ending frame after completion. It does not cause repeated playback. No repeat count is given here, so the normal run happens once. A final base width of 100% also preserves the full bar if animation is disabled.

Some people prefer less motion because moving content can be distracting or uncomfortable. Their device or browser can expose a reduced-motion preference. Use @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) to respond to that choice. This media feature is not a keyframe name or an animation delay value. Disabling this animation should still show the complete result, rather than leaving an empty bar. Do not make people wait for a moving graphic to obtain important information that could be available immediately in text.

A fraction tells how much of a total has passed. If two seconds have passed in a four-second run, 2 ÷ 4 is 0.5, or 50% of its time. With linear movement from zero width to full width, that also gives half the width. With ease-out, half the time does not necessarily give half the width: the timing function changes the relationship. The exercise uses ease-out, while its math question asks about a linear animation's time fraction. Keep elapsed time and displayed progress distinct whenever the movement is not linear.

For the project, define @keyframes fill from width: 0 to width: 100%, then apply fill to .bar. Keep the supplied 100% label. Add the reduced-motion media query, set animation: none there, and leave width: 100%. The checks choose the expected animation name based on the current preference and look for the query and label. Try both preference states using an appropriate browser testing control, and inspect the end state after motion finishes. A bar's width cannot establish actual upload success; it illustrates the supplied final state.
after: An animation changes a style over time. Keyframes describe the values at the start and end. This bar illustrates a download that is already complete; the animation does not perform the download.

The name `fill` connects the animation setting to the keyframes. `3s` means three seconds. `linear` gives a steady speed. `both` keeps the start frame during a delay and the end frame after the animation finishes.
The reduced-motion rule turns the animation off when someone asks for less motion. The normal `width: 100%` still shows the full bar.
Keep the supplied 100% text label visible. People should be able to read the result without judging the bar's width.
With steady, linear movement, halfway through the time means halfway through the width change. With `ease-out`, the movement slows near the end, so those halves need not match.
For the project, name the animation `fill`. Start at zero width and end at full width. Keep the result visible when motion is off.

before: Create an animation named fill with @keyframes. Make it grow from zero width to full width.
Keep the text label visible with the final percentage.
Use prefers-reduced-motion to check whether the user wants less movement. If so, turn off the animation and leave the bar full.
after: Create keyframes named `fill`, from zero width to full width.
Keep the final percentage label visible.
Turn off the animation for reduced motion and leave the bar full.

before: The animation name in `.bar` must match the `@keyframes` name.
Give keyframes a `from` and `to` state for width.
Inside the reduced-motion query, set `animation: none` and keep width at 100%.
after: The animation name must match the keyframe name.
Use `from` and `to` for the start and end widths.
Keep a normal width of 100% when the animation is off.

before.question: A completed-download bar stops animating for reduced motion. What should remain visible?
choices: No result, because the animation is the download
The complete bar and its 100% text label
An empty bar until motion is enabled
before.explanation: The animation illustrates an already-complete result. Disabling motion must not hide that result; CSS motion does not perform the download.

after.question: What should remain when reduced motion turns the completed-download animation off?
choices: No result, because the animation does the download
The full bar and its 100% text label
An empty bar until motion is on
after.explanation: The download is already complete. Turning off motion should keep that result visible.

project.title: A progress animation
project.task: Animate the completed bar and keep the same clear result when reduced motion is requested.
project.done_when: The animation ends at full width, and the full bar and 100% label remain when motion is off.
